data.name: Summer Nightmare
data.detailed_description:
Features


  • 41,566 words
  • 4 Endings
  • 9 Character CG
  • 55+ illust CGs
  • 35+ Original BGs
  • 11+ BGMs
  • 12 SFXs

Story


One day, a boy, Riel, has a nightmare. inside the dream there is a school just like in real where terrifying things continues to happen.
Being chased by a blood-soaked medusa, his friends are killed.
Students foam teams just to fight each other.
...this was a beginning of [Nightmare Game].

After inference of collected hints, they can end this game.
the [Broadcast] will tell about where Hints are, and friends' death.
they were programmed to bring them to death.

is the [Broadcast] from my mind? and what happened in dreams is connected to reality.
when someone dies in my dream- so do in reality. can Riel finish the game?

Summer Nightmare is a Mystery Survival adventure in dreams, surrounding Riel.
Protect friends, teacher and yourself!

『Those who happen to behold Medusa, are destined to be killed by someone.』

Gameplay Notes


  • You can change the language in Settings.
  • If you can not hear the game sound, increase the volume in the settings

reviews.review:
Summer Nightmare is a horror visual novel that turns the familiar idea of a bad dream into a deadly mystery where events during sleep can have consequences in the real world. Developed by Team Summer Nightmare and published by Elkibe Games, it follows Riel, a boy who becomes trapped in a disturbing Nightmare Game involving his school, friends, and teacher. Its strongest qualities come from its unsettling premise and constant uncertainty rather than complicated gameplay, making it primarily an experience for players who enjoy reading, making choices, and gradually uncovering the rules behind a supernatural mystery.

Riel initially finds himself dreaming about a school resembling the one he knows, but any sense of familiarity quickly disappears. Students are placed in dangerous situations, alliances become unreliable, and a frightening Medusa-like presence becomes connected to the deaths occurring around them. The situation becomes considerably more serious once Riel realizes that dying inside the nightmare can mean dying in reality as well. This gives the story an effective sense of urgency because escaping the dream is no longer simply a matter of waking up.

A particularly interesting element is the mysterious Broadcast system. Announcements reveal clues and information about deaths within the Nightmare Game, but their true origin remains uncertain. Riel begins wondering whether these messages are somehow coming from his subconscious or whether an outside entity is controlling the nightmare. The story further complicates matters with the rule surrounding Medusa, where seeing the creature supposedly means the victim will eventually be killed by another person. This shifts some of the fear away from monsters and toward the other characters, creating paranoia about who can actually be trusted.

Gameplay follows the traditional visual novel formula, with reading and choices forming the core experience. Summer Nightmare contains a script of roughly 41,000 words, giving the story enough space to establish its characters, mysteries, deaths, and supernatural rules. Player decisions can eventually lead toward four different endings, adding replay value for anyone interested in discovering alternative outcomes. The branching structure fits the premise particularly well because experimenting with different decisions can reveal how apparently minor choices influence Riel's fate and the survival of those around him.

Visually, the game uses an anime-inspired presentation accompanied by a considerable collection of illustrations and backgrounds. It includes numerous event CGs, character artwork, and more than thirty backgrounds, allowing the locations and important story moments to change frequently enough that the experience does not feel like staring at the same handful of screens. The contrast between colorful visual novel artwork and scenes involving violence, blood, death, and psychological distress can make some moments surprisingly uncomfortable. Players sensitive to gore should be aware that the game does not restrict itself to mild supernatural scares.

Sound design is comparatively modest. A limited selection of background music and sound effects is used to reinforce threatening scenes and major developments. It works reasonably well within the game's small-scale presentation, although greater audio variety could have made longer reading sessions more atmospheric. There is also no extensive voice performance carrying the dialogue, so much of the experience depends upon the player's willingness to read substantial amounts of text.

The writing is where Summer Nightmare shows both its ambition and its limitations. The underlying ideas are genuinely interesting, especially the connection between dreams and reality, the mysterious announcements, the rules surrounding death, and the uncertainty over who is controlling everything. However, some dialogue and English phrasing can feel awkward. Certain explanations and transitions are also less polished than they could be, occasionally making the story confusing when it should be mysterious. The number of supernatural concepts introduced can further complicate the narrative, particularly when several rules and revelations appear close together.

On the positive side, the game is technically undemanding. Its visual novel format means it requires very little computing power compared with most modern games. Steam Deck compatibility, however, is officially Unverified, meaning there is no confirmed Valve compatibility rating guaranteeing that every aspect works properly on the handheld. Given the lightweight visual novel structure, it may still be possible to run it through Steam Deck's compatibility environment, but players should not interpret that as official Verified or Playable status.

Summer Nightmare ultimately succeeds more through imagination than refinement. The concept of a nightmare capable of killing people in reality provides a strong foundation, while the supernatural rules, multiple endings, violent incidents, broadcasts, and uncertainty surrounding Medusa keep the mystery moving. Its weaknesses come from uneven writing, occasionally confusing storytelling, limited audio presentation, and the overall roughness expected from a relatively small independent project.

For players who enjoy supernatural visual novels and can overlook some presentation and writing imperfections, there is enough here to justify exploring the Nightmare Game and pursuing its different conclusions. Being free makes its shortcomings easier to accept, and its substantial script and multiple endings provide more content than its modest appearance might suggest. It is not an especially polished horror experience, but its unusual mixture of dreams, murder, paranoia, and branching outcomes gives it a memorable identity.

Rating: 6/10
